title: Yvette Fielding shares horrific injury on Most Haunted and 2 dead stars she won't contact
excerpt: EXCLUSIVE: The First Lady of the Paranormal revealed what happened when she approached the famous London landmark.
content:
As the "First Lady of the Paranormal", Yvette Fielding has investigated some of Britain's most haunted locations - but there's one historic landmark viewers won't be seeing her explore on screen anytime soon. Yvette, 58, who has presented paranormal reality show Most Haunted for almost a quarter of a century, approached the Tower of London about bringing her team in for an overnight investigation only to discover there was one rather significant obstacle. "They said, 'We love Most Haunted. We absolutely love it. What a great show!'" she recalls. "

"And they said, 'Well, what would you do [during filming]?' I said, 'Well, I've got to say, is there anybody there?' Their response draws a loud laugh from Yvette at the memory.

"'Oh no, you can't do that. We can't actively encourage the ghosts'," she recalls. "And I thought, fair enough. You don't want to scare members of the public. I get that."

"Despite the rejection, she hasn't been put off investigating London's most famous historic buildings. In fact, there is another landmark on her wish list, and this one has a rather more musical connection.

"I'm a huge Beatles fan. I would love to spend the night with my team at Abbey Road Studios, because I think there's so much energy there that we would get some really good stuff," she says.

"I think I would probably... I don't know what I'd do with myself. I would be fangirling a ghost. Many ghosts," she giggles. "I would be jittery and so excited."

Yvette's enthusiasm for paranormal investigations isn't just for the cameras. The former Blue Peter presenter is genuinely animated as she discusses her work, and her passion is evident as she recalls some of her most thrilling encounters.

It was very different when she started out, confessing she was a "quivering wreck" at the beginning.

"When I look at the first programme now, it makes me howl with laughter because you can see how terrified I am," she says. "Now, if there's a noise or a bang, I do still jump, or the occasional scream will come out. Not as bad as I used to, but [now] I'll run towards it."

Her enthusiasm might seem surprising given some of the horrific experiences she's witnessed. One, in particular, stands out.

The programme was broadcasting simultaneously across the UK and America when she witnessed three members of the crew being physically cut and scratched. One of them suffered a particularly serious injury to his leg. "He got deeply cut. You could see the bone in the bottom half of his leg, and he had to be rushed off to accident and emergency," she recalls.

The experience left her so shaken that she could barely continue presenting. "I just need to leave. I can't cope any more," she remembers saying, as colleagues speaking into her earpiece urged her to take a breath.

After taking several months away from the show, she eventually decided that if she was going to continue investigating the paranormal, she needed to understand it properly.

She began researching historical accounts of violent hauntings, including reports of bite marks, severe burns, scratches and welts. Rather than putting her off, this changed the way she approached the work.

"Now, if we get any scratches or anything like that, I get so excited," she admits. "I'm scared, but I'm excited at the same time because this is some real phenomena that we're capturing."

Yet despite her fascination with the afterlife, there are two famous figures she has deliberately never tried to contact. Chatting over Zoom, Yvette reveals she's sitting at comedy legend Eric Morecambe's writing desk, complete with the comedian's typewriter and hat. She moves her camera to show it fully. She also owns one of John Lennon's typewriters.

But despite having such personal connections to two famous figures from the past, she has never attempted to contact either of the celebrity giants.

"I've never asked. I've never gone, 'Is there anybody there?' Purely, I just wouldn't want to do that. It's not respectful for the family members," she explains. "I would love to, but I'm not going to. If he's here, he's here."

It is an interesting distinction for someone whose career has been built around investigating the dead. Yvette is fascinated by the possibility of making contact, but believes there is a line between curiosity and respect that should not be crossed.

For all her enthusiasm, she is also frustrated that paranormal activity is not taken more seriously by the scientific community. She has repeatedly invited scientists to join investigations, believing unexplained knocking and tapping could offer an opportunity for further research.

In the meantime, her enthusiasm shows no sign of fading. A new series of Most Haunted has just launched on Pluto TV, while the team is already filming the series after that.

Away from the paranormal, Yvette is turning her attention to a rather different kind of energy drain, fronting a campaign by non-profit Smart Energy GB aimed at helping Britain's small businesses tackle wasted energy.

"The campaign really touched a nerve with me because I've owned small businesses, from tea rooms to production companies, worked in telly and had businesses whilst being in telly," she says. "And when Smart Energy did the survey, it said about 60% of small business owners are finding it really hard to sleep at night because they're worried about their bills.

"That actually really got to me, and I thought that's awful. We've got to do everything we can to keep our small businesses going. But it's so funny, since starting doing this campaign I'm really annoying my husband because at night I'm going, 'Turn that off and unplug that. Why is that on?' So I've become a bit of a nightmare with it," she laughs.

Next May will mark 25 years since the launch of Most Haunted, which was created by Yvette and her husband Karl Beattie. It's a milestone she still finds astonishing, given how difficult it was to get the show off the ground.

The team initially struggled to find a broadcaster willing to take a chance on the idea, funding the pilot themselves. They paid the crew, who were friends, with beer and pizza, before spending money on a professional edit. Even then, nobody wanted to buy it. The breakthrough came when a friend of a friend, who was a senior figure at Flextech Television, then owner of Living TV, watched the pilot.

"He just went, 'Yeah, I'll have that. This just might be mad enough to work'," Yvette remembers.

When they eventually went into meetings with Living TV, the executives questioned whether there would be enough haunted locations to sustain a series. Yvette and the team arrived with a huge pile of papers, each listing a different location.

"It must have been 10 years' worth," she says. "They were looking [at it saying], 'This can't be real', and we were going, 'Yes it is. These are all verified, these are all haunted locations'."

The list still hasn't run dry, and Yvette says people continue to contact the team with reports of activity in their homes and other locations, often asking them to come and help.

"I just want to go in there and find out who it is, why they're causing paranormal activity to occur. Do they need help? Find out who they are, their names, the dates and all of that. I love that."

For someone who once needed months away from the cameras after a frightening investigation, it is quite a transformation. Yvette Fielding is clearly not ready to hang up her paranormal equipment... although the Tower of London will have to wait.
